summary: Existing I.2 combines human perishing and exhaustion; JTM 1.3/18 supplies explicit death, while 2/47 is labour-related hyperbole. These are retained under the inherited number rather than renumbered or split without more evidence.
I Preterit Intransitive halək can describe a present deteriorating state at 53/3 as well as a completed death; source translation does not change the glossary form box.
III Infectum mahlakle at 84/5 is a purpose clause with a target indexed by -le, despite matching the spelling of a citation Preterit base. No Preterit box is created from that spelling.
The current parsed Infectum label is already standardized; the raw Infeсtum has a Cyrillic character. New labels use Infectum, while inherited raw text remains unchanged.

Jan Beṯ-Şawoce has no edition translation. English accompanying the added examples is the supplied project machine translation, copied and cut without retranslation; lexical decisions rest on the Turoyo.
The new data add L-series past forms to III, which round 1 had only exemplified in Infectum. Nonhuman destruction preserves the inherited causing-ruin meaning.
mahlakwole contains the a-vowel of mahlakle and a final L-agent candidate; the temporal English 'used to' cannot establish Infectum-wa.
Mahlakke plausibly reflects k+l assimilation with a plural L-agent. The exact antecedent may be the immediately preceding pests or the entire calamity series.
Do speakers distinguish a narrower death sense from labour-related exhaustion within I.2? The present small sample retains both in their inherited sense.
Confirm the range of I.1 weggehen, which has no independent simple-departure attestation in this supplied sample.
Jan 2.33/5411: confirm mahlak-wo-le as Preterit-wa with third-person L-agent; the alternative Infectum-wa reading would need a defensible patient-suffix analysis.
Jan 3.11/118: confirm the plural agent ending of Mahlakke and whether pests or all the preceding calamities are its antecedent.

summary: Threatened destruction of a household and ruining a priest through slander retain verderben; social consequences need no new participant-specific sense.
Smallpox and a series of calamities or pests act as destructive causes affecting children or local people. These support verderben without a new lexical sense.
